Any given AV technology will have unique fallback behaviors in the case of an internal vehicle fault—determined and engineered by the technology provider. The OMA would provide minimum requirements for various types of fallback response at the fleet and system level that a technology provider would need to comply with. Examples of typical fallback responses include moving to the roadway shoulder to stop, driving across operating lanes to stop at a curbfront, or 2 Examples of potentially relevant safety standards include those from the International Electrotechnical Commission (2009, 2011), UL (2023), and SAE International (2021a). 34 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. stopping within the vehicle’s current operating lane. Such guidelines would also include protocol for reporting failure conditions to the OMA so alerts may be appropriately provided to other roadway users and emergency response if needed. Further, the safety protocols would guide remote operator response procedures if a vehicle or subsystem failure requires intervention by what SAE calls a “remote assistant” (or, for some technologies, a remote tele-operator) or by emergency response personnel. This is particularly critical for the OMA to ensure full coordination between the fleet operator’s response team and the actions and protocols of police, fire, and first responders. 3.3.4 Role of Intelligent Roadway Infrastructure A key conclusion of the assessment of the 10 early deployments was that keeping the fleet AVs safely operating at speeds as close as possible to other traffic operations is essential to reducing crashes, especially rear-end collisions on the approach to signalized intersections. This issue of reduction in speed was common in complex environments such as intersections with multiple lanes, significant turning movements, and nonvehicle traffic such as pedestrians, bicyclists, and various forms of micromobility. Large-scale AV deployments within complex AMD operating environments such as multimodal intersections may require sophisticated, advanced sensing and control technology to support and augment the AV sensing capabilities and coordinate all modes of traffic for safety and efficiency, referred to as IRI. Further, IRI communication protocols, such as those outlined in the principles of cooperative driving automation (SAE J3216), should be beneficially integrated into any fleet AV control systems if adopted by the OMA. For example, the IRI may detect system- level hazards beyond the sensor range of any fleet AV and provide directives to any fleet AVs approaching an intersection to either 1) decrease speed, move to the side of the road, or come to a halt within their travel lane or 2) avoid a particular route experiencing trouble, as appropriate for the “over-the-horizon” hazard. Infrastructure sensing is being used to document and validate AV performance and conformance to policy, even extending to emergency responder “body cams.” This independent record of vehicular performance is growing increasingly critical to identify and remedy AV performance issues. Based on the lessons learned at Colorado School of Mines, Rivium, and other early deployment sites, mitigating speed differentials between AVs and human-operated vehicles is critical.
